title: Kara and kangha, daily

lines: A STEEL BAND AT THE WRIST.
cards: A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the fridge. An alarm with a label.
People lean on small things to hold big intentions, because big intentions slip away by lunchtime.

Watch a Sikh at a kitchen counter, reaching for a knife to cut vegetables, and you might catch the light on a plain steel band at the wrist. At the end of the day you might see a small comb tucked into the knot of hair.
Two of the five Ks are small enough to forget you're wearing them. Sikhs wear them so they won't forget.

teach.h: THE KARA: PLAIN STEEL, NO END.
teach.b: Start with the kara. It's a plain bracelet, usually of steel or iron, worn on the wrist by Sikhs who keep the five Ks, and by other Sikhs too. It isn't jewelry: no gold, no gems, no clasp.
Early on this path, it came with a question: what are these hands doing? Sikhs often point to two things about it.
Its shape is a circle, with no beginning and no end, which they take as a reminder of the One without beginning or end.

teach.h: IT SITS WHERE THE HAND BEGINS.
teach.b: And its place is the wrist, right where the hand begins. Before the hand takes, strikes, signs or gives, it passes the kara: a small steel question on the way. Is this an act the Guru would stand behind?
Now the kangha. You met it a few days ago as a tool of care. Today, see it as a reminder.

teach.h: THE KANGHA: A LIFE KEPT IN ORDER.
teach.b: It lives in the hair all day, a quiet sign that a Sikh life is meant to be kept in order, clean and tended, not tangled and neglected.

Some Sikhs pair the two in their own way: a touch of the kara before work, a moment with the kangha at night. Neither is magic. The code rejects charms and lucky objects, as you heard earlier on this path.
The kara and the kangha protect no one by themselves; they work only when they're noticed. That's why they're worn every day.
A reminder you see once a year is a decoration.
A reminder on your wrist all day is a practice.

how: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a plain steel kara on the wrist and keep a small kangha in the hair every day, and Sikhs often describe them as reminders of the Guru's way.

o: lucky charms that keep a Sikh safe from harm
a steel bracelet and small comb, worn as reminders
gifts given to a bride at a Sikh wedding

games.q: two small reminders: tap the pairs.
p: a small comb kept in the hair

s: the kara is a piece of jewelry
it's plain, usually steel or iron: no gold, no gems, no clasp.
the kara protects the wearer like a charm
the code rejects charms. the kara works only when it's noticed, as a reminder.
the kara sits where the hand begins
so before the hand acts, it passes the kara.

games.q: you wear a kara, and your hand is about to sign something you're unsure of. what do Sikhs say the kara asks?
o: whether today is a lucky day.
whether this is an act the Guru would stand behind.
games.why: the kara sits where the hand begins. Sikhs take it as a small question resting on the way to every act.

practice: Rest the fingers of one hand on the other wrist: if you wear a kara, feel the cool steel; if not, feel your pulse, or just the bone.
Picture the next thing your hands will do, pick up a phone, open a door, hold someone, and ask quietly whether it's something you'd stand behind. Stay there, fingers on your wrist, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Kara and kangha. The steel bracelet at the wrist and the small comb in the hair: two of the five Ks, worn every day as reminders. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the plain steel bracelet, one of the five Ks.

carryVoice: Your line: touch and remember. A reminder only works when it's noticed, day after day. Until tomorrow.
